content:
This year, on August 9th, the Observatory recorded the highest temperature in history since records began in 1884 — 36.9 degrees Celsius, while Sheung Shui reached an even higher 39.8 degrees Celsius in the afternoon after three o'clock. In the scorching heat, I hid inside a long, narrow house, leaving only a crack in the window for air. Under extreme heat, hot air really does rush into the home. So, the balcony doors and the living room windows were all shut tight. I live on a mid-floor flat between two small hills; except at noon, the sun is kept away from all sides. Even without air conditioning, the three ceiling fans in the house spin in their creaking rhythm, bringing cool breezes. Amid the Hong Kong-style heatwave, I have much to be grateful for.

Under the hottest weather in history, I hid at home doing laundry. After one o'clock in the afternoon, I washed two long, large bedsheets and duvet covers, four pairs of jeans, and a pile of T-shirts. Two hours later, I flipped the bedsheets and duvet covers to dry on the other side. As a result, after six o'clock in the evening, I held the warm laundry — as if just taken out of a large washing machine at a laundromat — and placed it on the bed. It felt as though I had never in half a century experienced such naturally sun-dried, clean laundry. I should have been worrying about my friends under the fierce sun, but only by washing the clothes load by load could I offset just a little of the hateful intensity of the scorching sun.

August has become a nightmare. I do not know how many more times it will take to break free from that repetitive summer of partings. In a dream one night, I swaggered forward, twisting my mother's arm as I walked, saying: "My little mummy." I gripped her tightly with great joy. Then, I saw a mysterious woman ahead, draped in a long, deep maroon cloak. Subconsciously I did not want to see her face clearly, but eventually, the camera in the dream kept zooming in on her face — she was a strange woman I did not recognise. Until I woke from the dream, a feeling of triumphant elation surfaced, and what I remembered was: I have dreamed of my mother again.

On the evening of August 10th, 2020, our whole family, singing hymns, kissed my mother's forehead and bid her farewell — that was a full stop. Yet, to truly let go is a lesson hard to learn in a lifetime. The unwillingness to part is a hidden wound. Six years on, there remain countless moments of regret in the smallest details, and in my mind, I keep replaying the days leading up to that day six years ago.

The regret and reluctance of parting — whether early or late, regardless of age — will appear at different stages of life. A female student in a writing class wrote in her essay about her grandmother who had passed away. It was a piece of remembrance, mourning, or regret. When she was even younger, she despised living with her grandmother in the countryside. During the day, with the boundless energy of a little imp, she would bicker with her grandmother. When her grandmother pinched her ear, she would strike back, letting her grandmother feel the pain she had felt. Then, through a crack in the door, the little child saw her frail, elderly grandmother secretly wipe away tears. That very night, the girl fell ill with a fever, and walked dazedly to her grandmother, saying: "I feel awful."

"Awful" simply means uncomfortable — that is how a child experiences sickness. She had a high fever, her whole body burning hot. Without a word, her grandmother found clean clothes for her to change into, and immediately carried her on her back to the hospital to wait to see a doctor. The scent of medicated oil, once despised, vaguely carried her to the hospital. Before long, somehow, that scent of medicated oil disappeared, and the little girl sat alone near the service counter waiting. Then, a few adults asked her: "Where are your family?" As she spoke, she began to cry, until the scent of medicated oil drifted close again, and she finally calmed down and waited properly for the doctor to give her an injection and medicine.

Back home, the scent of medicated oil was as usual, but seemed to have lost its sharpness. From the kitchen came the sound of meat being chopped on the cutting board, and the aroma of rice porridge wafting from the hot pot. The meaning of life in this world needs no elaborate explanation — it is as simple and clear as this.

I wonder, who is it today who cooks porridge for the sick?

When I was little, it was mostly my father, sometimes my mother, who would have the patience to hand-chop beef and cook porridge for me. This was a sick-day menu, and only I was allowed to eat it. Sometimes, after seeing the doctor, I would pre-order this kind of meat porridge: "I want scallion and beef porridge." It was a sick-day privilege. Now, there is no one who would cook this particular porridge for me, and when I get sick, I will never eat this kind of beef porridge again.

"When you're sick these days, just order Food Panda," a friend said. Some friends also cook plain porridge or fish porridge for their wives. "Sometimes I cook minced meat porridge too." "Hand-chopped, not using a blender." "It only takes a few minutes to chop it up." Because of a pot of porridge, one feels cherished.

"In a lifetime, not many people will cook porridge for you when you are sick. After growing up, the most likely scenario is that you cook it for others. These things, many people have already experienced. Whatever thoughts you may have, bid them a proper farewell, speak the words in your heart, and those who read it will feel comforted for you." I said to the female student. She looked at me, a glint of light flashing in her eyes.

An essay about a grandmother can bring comfort. My father, my mother, my grandmother... these are stories we naturally know how to write.

The female student's strength is not simply good writing — she seized upon the medicated oil as the central thread, and around that thread, conveyed her true feelings toward her closest kin. She need not have been the one who loved her grandmother most, but that time together, arranged by fate, means she can never forget everything her grandmother did for her, nor fail to understand that people grow up in such unwitting ways. In the end, she submitted a deeply moving and "heart-wrenching" essay.

The medicated oil went from being detestable, reliable, shameful, to a thing of remembrance. It turns out that on the little girl's first day of primary school, she was laughed at by classmates for smelling of medicated oil, who called her a country bumpkin. She ran home crying and sternly ordered her grandmother to wash all the clothes thoroughly with heavy loads of laundry detergent from top to bottom. Grandmother held the clothes and wept. The girl had been eight months old when her grandmother began raising her, and as she grew up and went to school, exposed to the outside world, the little granddaughter seemed to become a different person, hurting her grandmother's heart. After returning to live with her mother, one day when grandmother had already developed dementia (Alzheimer's disease), the girl went with her mother to visit her. She discovered that she was no longer "recognised" by her grandmother.

"You can't be my granddaughter. She doesn't like talking to me," the old grandmother said to the girl.

Life is both real and cruel. Have I ever been this cruel to my own mother? It seems not. Or perhaps I have, and like the female student, I simply do not know. Family members sometimes hurt one another. The key point is, afterwards, have we come to understand love more deeply?
